lessons.title: Compounding: money that grows itself
cards: Compounding means earning returns on your past returns. Your money grows, then that growth grows too. Over long stretches, this snowball does most of the work.

cards.q: You invest $1,000 once and it grows 8% a year. Roughly what is it worth after 30 years?
cards.why: Compounded at 8% for 30 years, $1,000 becomes about $10,063. Without compounding (8% of the original $1,000 each year) you'd only reach $3,400.

cards.text: Try it: move the sliders. Notice how adding years changes the result far more than adding a few dollars a month.

cards: A handy shortcut is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly return to estimate how many years it takes to double. At 8%, money doubles about every 9 years.
Compounding needs two things you control: starting early and not interrupting it. Pulling money out or stopping for years resets the snowball.

quiz.q: What is compounding?
a: Earning returns on your past returns
quiz.why: Growth on top of growth is what makes long-term investing so powerful.

quiz.q: Using the rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 6% a year?
quiz.why: 72 divided by 6 is 12.

quiz.q: Which usually matters most for compounding?
a: How many years the money grows
Picking a stock with a low share price
quiz.why: Time is the engine. Each extra year grows on everything before it.

lessons.title: Dollar-cost averaging
cards: Dollar-cost averaging means investing the same amount on a regular schedule, like $100 every month, whatever the price is doing.
Because the amount stays fixed, you automatically buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when they are high. It also takes the guesswork out of picking the perfect day.

cards.text: Try it: make the dip in month 3 deeper and watch your average cost per share.

cards.q: Prices drop 30% right after you start investing $100 a month. What happens to your next purchases?
a: You get more shares for the same $100
You get the same number of shares
cards.why: Lower prices mean each $100 buys more shares, which lowers your average cost.

cards: Historically, investing a lump sum right away has beaten spreading it out about two times out of three, because markets rise more often than they fall. Dollar-cost averaging shines when you invest from each paycheck anyway, and it makes drops feel less scary.

quiz.q: What does dollar-cost averaging mean?
a: Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule
Only buying when prices hit a new low
quiz.why: Same amount, same schedule, whatever the price.

quiz.q: When prices fall, a fixed $100 monthly investment buys...
quiz.why: Cheaper shares mean your $100 goes further.

quiz.q: Why do many people like dollar-cost averaging?
a: It removes the pressure of timing the market
quiz.why: Nothing guarantees a profit, but a schedule takes emotion and timing out of it.

lessons.title: Why small fees add up
cards: Funds charge a yearly fee called the expense ratio. It's a percent of what you invest, taken out a little at a time, so you never see a bill.

cards.q: You invest $10,000 for 30 years at 7% a year. About how much does a 1% yearly fee cost you compared with a 0.05% fee?
cards.why: With a 0.05% fee you'd end with about $75,000. With a 1% fee, about $56,300. The fee is charged every year on a growing balance, so it compounds against you.

cards.text: Try it: slide the fee and watch the gap grow.

cards: Index funds that track the S&P 500 often charge 0.10% a year or less. Actively managed funds usually charge more, and most of them trail their index over long periods.
Other costs to watch: trading commissions (most big US brokers now charge $0 for stocks and ETFs), account fees and advisory fees. Check the fee before you buy any fund.

quiz.q: What is an expense ratio?
a: A fund's yearly fee as a percent of your money
The price of one share of a fund
How much the fund grew last year
quiz.why: An expense ratio of 0.10% costs $1 a year for every $1,000 invested.

quiz.q: Fund A charges 0.05% and fund B charges 1%. They hold the same stocks. Which likely leaves you with more after 30 years?
quiz.why: Same holdings, lower fee: more of the growth stays with you.

quiz.q: Why do small fees matter so much over decades?
a: They're taken every year, so they compound against you
They only apply in the first year
quiz.why: A fee shrinks your balance every year, and the missing money can't grow.

lessons.title: Inflation: why cash slowly shrinks
cards: Inflation is prices rising over time. When a coffee goes from $3 to $3.30, each dollar buys a little less.

cards.q: Prices rise 3% a year. About how much buying power does $1,000 of cash under the mattress lose in 20 years?
cards.why: After 20 years of 3% inflation, $1,000 buys what about $554 buys today. It's still $1,000, but it buys less.

cards.text: Try it: see what cash is really worth after years of inflation.

cards: That's why long-term money is usually invested rather than kept as cash. Over long periods, US stocks have grown faster than inflation, even though some years they lose value.
Cash still has a job. Money you might need soon, like an emergency fund, belongs somewhere safe even if inflation nibbles at it. High-yield savings accounts and Treasury bills can help it keep up.

quiz.q: What is inflation?
quiz.why: When prices rise, each dollar buys less.

quiz.q: Prices rise 3% a year. What happens to cash that earns nothing?
a: It buys a little less each year
quiz.why: The number stays the same, but its buying power shrinks.

quiz.q: Which money is fine to keep in cash despite inflation?
a: An emergency fund you might need soon
Retirement money for 30 years from now
quiz.why: Money you may need soon should be safe and easy to reach.

lessons.title: Before you invest: the money checklist
cards: Investing works best on a solid base. Before buying stocks, many people make sure a few things are in place first.

cards.text: Put these steps in the order many personal finance guides suggest:
items: Pay off high-interest debt like credit cards
Invest more for the long term
cards.why: A small cushion keeps surprises off your credit card, an employer match is free money, credit card interest often tops 20%, and then long-term investing can do its work.

cards: An emergency fund is cash for surprises: a car repair, a medical bill, a lost job. A common target is three to six months of essential expenses, kept somewhere safe and easy to reach.

cards.q: Your credit card charges 24% interest. Stocks have averaged roughly 10% a year over the long run. What's the better use of an extra $500?
cards.why: Paying off a 24% card is like earning a guaranteed 24%. Stocks average far less, and nothing about them is guaranteed.

cards: Then think about time. Money you need within a few years usually shouldn't be in stocks, because a drop could hit right when you need it.

quiz.q: What is an emergency fund for?
a: Unexpected costs like repairs or losing a job
quiz.why: It keeps a surprise from becoming debt or a forced sale.

quiz.q: Why pay off a 24% credit card before investing?
a: Card interest stops after a year
quiz.why: Few investments beat a sure 24%.

quiz.q: Money you need in the next year should usually be...
a: Put in a single growth stock
quiz.why: Short-term money can't wait for a market recovery.

lessons.title: Retirement accounts: 401(k) and IRA
cards: In the US, retirement accounts give you tax breaks for investing. The two most common are the 401(k), offered through a job, and the IRA, which you open yourself.

Traditional accounts let you put money in before tax and pay tax when you withdraw in retirement. Roth accounts work the other way: you pay tax now, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.

cards.text: Match each term to what it means:
pairs: A retirement plan offered by your employer
A retirement account you open yourself
Pay tax now, withdraw tax-free later
Extra money your job adds when you save

cards.q: Your job matches 100% of what you put in, up to 4% of your salary. You earn $50,000 and contribute $2,000 a year. How much does your employer add?
cards.why: 4% of $50,000 is $2,000, and a 100% match doubles it: an instant 100% return before any market growth.

cards: Each account has a yearly contribution limit set by the IRS, and taking money out early can mean taxes and penalties. Check the current rules, or ask a tax professional about your situation.

quiz.q: Which account is usually offered through your job?
quiz.why: Employers sponsor 401(k) plans. IRAs you open on your own.

quiz.q: With a Roth account, when do you pay tax?
quiz.why: You pay tax up front, and qualified withdrawals later are tax-free.

quiz.q: Why is an employer match valuable?
a: It's extra money added to what you save
It lets you skip taxes forever
quiz.why: It's part of your pay you only get if you contribute.

lessons.title: The P/E ratio: cheap or pricey?
cards: The price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) compares a stock's price with the company's yearly profit per share. A P/E of 20 means investors pay $20 for every $1 of yearly profit.

cards.text: Try it: change the share price and the profit per share.
Real numbers. Which of these do you think has the highest P/E right now? Tap your guess.

cards: A high P/E usually means investors expect fast growth. A low P/E can mean a bargain, or a business people expect to shrink. Compare companies in the same industry, not a bank with a chip maker.
P/E doesn't work when a company has no profit, so it's blank for many young companies. Forward P/E uses analysts' estimates of next year's profit instead.

quiz.q: A stock costs $50 and earns $2.50 per share a year. What's its P/E?
quiz.why: $50 divided by $2.50 is 20.

quiz.q: A high P/E usually signals that investors...
quiz.why: People pay more per dollar of profit when they expect profit to grow.

quiz.q: Why might a company show no P/E at all?
quiz.why: You can't divide by earnings that don't exist.

lessons.title: Market cap: how big is a company?
cards: Market capitalization (market cap) is the total value of all of a company's shares: the share price times the number of shares.

cards.q: Company A's stock costs $500. Company B's costs $50. Which company is bigger?
a: You can't tell from the share price alone
cards.why: Size is price times shares. A $50 stock with 10 billion shares ($500B) is far bigger than a $500 stock with 100 million shares ($50B).

cards.text: Guess which company is worth the most, then see the real values.

cards: Companies are often grouped by size: large caps (over about $10 billion), mid caps (about $2 to $10 billion) and small caps (under about $2 billion). Smaller companies can grow faster but usually swing more.

cards.text: Order these companies from smallest to largest:
cards.why: Market cap is how size is measured, from small caps up to the trillion-dollar giants.

quiz.q: How is market cap calculated?
a: Share price times number of shares
quiz.why: It's the value of every share added together.

quiz.q: A $20 stock with 5 billion shares has a market cap of...
quiz.why: $20 times 5 billion is $100 billion.

quiz.q: Compared with large caps, small-cap stocks usually...
quiz.why: Smaller businesses are less established, so their prices move more.

lessons.title: Profit margins: what a company keeps
cards: Revenue is the money coming in from sales. Profit margin tells you how much of each dollar is left after every cost.
A 25% profit margin means the company keeps 25 cents of every dollar of sales. A grocery chain might keep 2 or 3 cents. A big software company can keep 30 cents or more.

cards.text: Guess which one keeps the most of each sales dollar.

cards.q: Two companies each sell $10 billion a year. One has a 5% margin, the other 25%. How much more profit does the second make?
cards.why: 5% of $10B is $0.5B and 25% is $2.5B, a $2B difference.

cards: Watch the trend. Rising margins usually mean pricing power or better efficiency. Shrinking margins can mean rising costs or tougher competition.

quiz.q: A 10% profit margin means the company keeps...
a: 10 cents of every sales dollar as profit
quiz.why: Margin is profit divided by revenue.

quiz.q: Which business usually has thin margins?
a: A drug maker with a patented medicine
quiz.why: Grocers sell huge volumes at small markups.

quiz.q: Margins shrinking year after year can be a sign of...
quiz.why: Something is squeezing what's left of each sale.

lessons.title: Growth: is the business getting bigger?
cards: Revenue growth shows how fast a company's sales are rising compared with a year earlier. Investors pay up for companies that keep growing quickly for a long time.

cards.text: Guess which grew sales fastest in its latest quarter compared with a year earlier.

cards: Growth isn't everything. A company growing sales 40% a year while losing more money every year is riskier than one growing 10% with steady profit.

cards.q: A company's revenue grows 15% a year for 5 years. Roughly how much bigger are sales by the end?
cards.why: Growth compounds: 1.15 multiplied by itself 5 times is about 2.0, not 1.75.

cards: Look at several years, not one quarter. Earnings reports show revenue, and StockSight's stock pages show recent growth in plain English.

quiz.q: What does revenue growth measure?
a: How fast the stock price is rising
quiz.why: It compares sales now with sales a year earlier.

quiz.q: Which is usually the steadier business?
quiz.why: Profitable growth doesn't depend on raising more money to survive.

quiz.q: Sales grow 15% a year for 5 years. They roughly...
quiz.why: Compounding turns 15% a year into about 100% over five years.

lessons.title: Dividends: getting paid to own a stock
cards: Some companies share part of their profit with shareholders as cash payments called dividends, usually every three months.
The dividend yield is the yearly dividend divided by the share price. A $100 stock paying $3 a year yields 3%.

cards.text: Try it: how much yearly income would an investment produce?
Guess which pays the highest dividend yield right now.

cards: A very high yield can be a warning sign. Sometimes it means the price fell because investors expect the dividend to be cut. Fast-growing companies often pay little or nothing and reinvest instead.

quiz.q: A $50 stock pays $2 a year in dividends. What's its yield?
quiz.why: $2 divided by $50 is 4%.

quiz.q: Why might a fast-growing company pay no dividend?
quiz.why: Reinvesting can create more value than paying cash out.

quiz.q: An unusually high yield can be a sign that...
quiz.why: A falling price pushes the yield up, often for a reason.

lessons.title: Analyst ratings and price targets
cards: Analysts at banks and research firms study companies and publish ratings (buy, hold or sell) and a price target: where they think the stock could trade in about a year.

cards.text: Average analyst target compared with today's price. Guess which one analysts see the most upside in.

cards: Targets are educated guesses, not promises. They often change after the price has already moved, and analysts can all be wrong together.

cards.q: A stock trades at $100. Analyst targets range from $70 to $160, averaging $120. What does the wide range tell you?
a: Experts disagree a lot about this stock
cards.why: A wide spread of targets means a lot of uncertainty about the future.

cards: Use ratings as one input among many: how many analysts cover the stock, how wide their targets are, and whether the business numbers back them up.

quiz.q: What is a price target?
a: An analyst's estimate of where a stock could trade in a year
quiz.why: It's a forecast, and forecasts can be wrong.

quiz.q: Targets from $70 to $160 suggest...
quiz.why: The wider the range, the less sure the experts are.

quiz.q: How should you treat analyst ratings?
a: As one opinion among several inputs
quiz.why: Check them against the business numbers.

lessons.title: Debt and cash: can it weather a storm?
cards: A company's balance sheet lists what it owns, like cash, and what it owes, like debt. Too much debt can turn a bad year into a crisis.
Borrowing isn't always bad. Debt can fund growth, and steady businesses like utilities carry a lot of it safely. Trouble starts when profits can't easily cover the interest.

cards.q: Two companies each make $1 billion a year in profit. One owes $500 million, the other $20 billion. Which is in a tougher spot if sales drop?
cards.why: The heavily indebted company still owes its payments when profit shrinks.

cards.text: Match each term to what it means:
pairs: Money the company has on hand
Money it borrowed and must repay
Debt compared with what shareholders own

cards: Quick checks: Is cash bigger than debt? Is debt shrinking or growing? Could a few years of profit or cash flow pay it off?

quiz.q: When does debt become dangerous?
a: When profits can't easily cover the payments
Only when the stock price rises
quiz.why: Debt is fine until the payments outgrow what the business earns.

quiz.q: A company with more cash than debt is usually...
a: Better able to handle a bad year
quiz.why: Cash is a cushion when times get hard.

quiz.q: What does debt-to-equity compare?
quiz.why: It shows how much of the business is funded by borrowing.

lessons.title: Free cash flow: the cash that's left
cards: Profit on paper isn't the same as cash in the bank. Free cash flow is the cash a business generates after running its operations and paying for things like buildings and equipment.
Companies use free cash flow to pay dividends, buy back shares, pay down debt or invest in growth. Steady, rising free cash flow is one of the best signs of a healthy business.

cards.q: A company reports a profit, but its free cash flow has been negative for years. What could that mean?
a: It's spending more cash than it brings in
cards.why: Accounting profit can hide heavy spending. Cash going out faster than it comes in has to be funded somehow.

cards: Mature companies usually produce steady free cash flow. Young ones often burn cash while they grow, which is fine only if the growth eventually pays off.

quiz.q: What is free cash flow?
a: Cash left after running and investing in the business
Money raised by selling new shares
quiz.why: It's the cash the business truly produces.

quiz.q: What can a company do with free cash flow?
a: Pay dividends or buy back shares
quiz.why: It's the money available to reward owners or reinvest.

quiz.q: Negative free cash flow for years means...
a: The company is burning more cash than it makes
quiz.why: It has to borrow, sell shares or use savings to keep going.

lessons.title: Bull markets, bear markets and corrections
cards: A bull market is a long stretch of rising prices. A bear market is a fall of 20% or more from a recent high. A correction is a smaller drop of 10% to 20%.

cards.text: Match each name to what it means:
pairs: A small drop of a few percent
A 10% to 20% fall from a high
A long run of rising prices

cards.text: Real data: the S&P 500's biggest fall from a high in the last five years, and how long it took to recover.

cards: Since 1950, the S&P 500 has had a correction about every two years and a bear market roughly every six years. So far the broad US market has always gone on to new highs, though some recoveries took years. That isn't true of every single stock.

cards.q: The market just fell 15% from its high. What's that called?
cards.why: 10% to 20% is a correction. A bear market starts at 20%.

quiz.q: A bear market is a fall of at least...
quiz.why: 20% from the high is the common definition.

quiz.q: A 12% drop from a high is a...
quiz.why: Between 10% and 20% is a correction.

quiz.q: Has the broad US stock market recovered from past bear markets?
a: Yes, though some recoveries took years
quiz.why: It has always recovered so far, but patience was sometimes measured in years.

lessons.title: Interest rates and the Fed
cards: The Federal Reserve (the Fed) sets a key short-term interest rate in the US. It raises rates to cool inflation and cuts them to support a slowing economy.

Higher rates make borrowing more expensive for people and companies, which can slow spending and profits. They also make safer options like savings accounts and bonds more attractive compared with stocks.

cards.q: The Fed unexpectedly raises rates. Which stocks are often hit hardest?
a: Fast-growing companies whose profits are far in the future
Companies with lots of cash and steady profits
cards.why: Higher rates shrink what far-off profits are worth today, so stocks priced on future growth tend to react the most.

cards.text: Match each term to what it means:
pairs: The interest a bond pays as a percent of its price

cards: Markets often move more on what the Fed is expected to do than on the decision itself. When a change is widely expected, it may already be in prices.

quiz.q: Why does the Fed raise interest rates?
quiz.why: Pricier borrowing slows spending, which eases price rises.

quiz.q: Higher rates make borrowing...
quiz.why: Loans, mortgages and credit cards all cost more.

quiz.q: If a rate cut is widely expected, the stock market...
a: May have already priced it in
quiz.why: Prices react to surprises more than to expected news.

lessons.title: Sectors: the market's neighborhoods
cards: Stocks are grouped into 11 sectors, like Technology, Health Care, Financials and Energy. Companies in the same sector often move together because the same news affects them.

cards.text: Match each company to its sector:

cards: Some sectors are called defensive, like Consumer Staples (food and household goods) and Utilities, because people keep buying their products in a downturn. Cyclical sectors, like travel and cars, swing more with the economy.

cards.text: Defensive versus cyclical in real numbers. Guess which one swings the most.

cards.q: The economy slows into a recession. Which sector tends to hold up better?
cards.why: People still buy groceries and toothpaste when money is tight.

quiz.q: How many sectors does the standard system use?
quiz.why: The widely used GICS system has 11 sectors.

quiz.q: Which sector is usually considered defensive?
quiz.why: Demand for everyday essentials stays steady.

quiz.q: Why do stocks in the same sector often move together?
quiz.why: Oil prices move energy stocks, interest rates move banks, and so on.

cta.label: Filter by sector in the screener

lessons.title: Volatility and beta
cards: Volatility measures how much a price swings. A stock with 50% yearly volatility moves much further, up and down, than one with 15%.
Beta compares a stock's moves with the whole market. A beta of 1 moves about like the S&P 500, 1.5 about 50% more, and 0.5 about half as much.

cards.text: Guess which has the highest beta, then see the real ones.

cards.q: The market falls 10%. A stock with a beta of 2 would typically fall about...
cards.why: Beta of 2 means roughly twice the market's move, in either direction.

cards: Higher volatility isn't automatically bad: big swings can mean big gains too. But it means a wider range of outcomes, so many investors keep those positions smaller.

quiz.q: What does volatility measure?
quiz.why: It's the size of typical ups and downs.

quiz.q: A beta of 0.5 means the stock usually moves...
a: About half as much as the market
Twice as much as the market
quiz.why: Below 1 means calmer than the market.

quiz.q: Why keep volatile positions smaller?
quiz.why: A smaller position limits the damage of a big swing.

lessons.title: News, hype and the herd
cards: Prices react to news within seconds. By the time a headline reaches you, it's usually already in the price.
Hype spreads fast on social media. A stock that jumps 50% in a week on buzz alone can fall just as fast when attention moves on.

cards.q: A company beats earnings estimates, but the stock falls 8%. How is that possible?
a: Investors expected even more, or the outlook disappointed
cards.why: Prices reflect expectations. Good news that's less good than hoped can still push a stock down.

cards.text: Rank these from most to least reliable for company facts:
items: The company's official filings with the SEC
An anonymous post saying it will 10x
cards.why: Official filings are legally required to be accurate. Anonymous hype has no accountability at all.

cards: A good habit: when a stock is in the news, open its page and check whether the business numbers changed, or only the mood.

quiz.q: When you read a big headline, the price has usually...
quiz.why: Professional traders react in seconds.

quiz.q: A stock beats estimates and still falls. Why?
quiz.why: It's about results compared with what people expected.

quiz.q: Which source is most reliable for company facts?
quiz.why: Filings are checked and legally binding.

lessons.title: Market hours and order types
cards: The main US stock exchanges are open 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern time, Monday to Friday, except market holidays.
Many brokers also offer pre-market and after-hours trading. Fewer people trade then, so prices can jump around more and the gap between buy and sell prices (the spread) is wider.

cards.text: Match each order type to what it does:
pairs: Trade right away at the best available price
Only trade at your price or better
Sell automatically if the price falls to a set level
The gap between the best buy and sell prices

cards.q: You place a market order at 8 p.m. on a Friday. With most brokers, when does it fill?
a: When the market opens on Monday
cards.why: It waits for the next open and fills at whatever the price is then. A limit order protects you from a surprise opening price.

cards: Crypto is different: it trades 24 hours a day, every day, including weekends.

quiz.q: When are the main US stock markets open?
a: 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern, on weekdays
quiz.why: Regular hours are 9:30 to 4 Eastern, Monday to Friday.

quiz.q: Why can after-hours trading be riskier?
a: Fewer traders, so prices swing more
quiz.why: Thin trading means bigger jumps and wider spreads.

quiz.q: Which order protects you from paying more than you planned?
quiz.why: A limit order never fills above your price.

cta.label: Try an order in Paper Trade

lessons.title: Stock splits and buybacks
cards: In a stock split, a company gives shareholders more shares at a lower price. In a 4-for-1 split, one $400 share becomes four $100 shares. Your total stays $400.

cards.q: You own 10 shares at $300 and the company does a 3-for-1 split. What do you have?
cards.why: Three times the shares at a third of the price: still $3,000.

cards: Splits don't change what the company is worth. They just make each share cheaper, which some investors like.
A buyback is when a company uses cash to buy its own shares. With fewer shares, each remaining share owns a bigger slice of the profit.

cards.q: A company earns $1 billion and has 1 billion shares, so it earns $1 per share. It buys back 10% of its shares and profit stays the same. What happens to earnings per share?
cards.why: $1 billion split across 900 million shares is about $1.11 each.

quiz.q: Does a 2-for-1 split change the total value of your shares?
a: No, you get twice the shares at half the price
quiz.why: The pie is cut into more slices. It doesn't get bigger.

quiz.q: What is a buyback?
a: A company buying its own shares
A refund for a bad stock
A broker buying your shares back
quiz.why: The company retires shares using its cash.

quiz.q: Why can buybacks lift earnings per share?
a: The same profit is split across fewer shares
quiz.why: Fewer shares means more profit per share.

lessons.title: Time in the market beats timing it
cards: Jumping out before drops and back in before rises sounds smart, but almost nobody does it consistently, professionals included.

cards.text: Real S&P 500 data: what if you'd missed just the best days of the last five years?

cards: Many of the best days happen right after the worst ones, often in the middle of scary markets. People who sell in a panic often miss the rebound.

cards.q: The market drops 25%. Historically, what has usually worked out better for long-term investors?
a: Moving everything into last year's top stock
cards.why: Recoveries often start suddenly, and sellers usually miss the first and biggest days.

cards: A plan you can stick to, like investing a set amount every month and leaving it alone, beats a brilliant plan you abandon in a panic.

quiz.q: Why is timing the market so hard?
a: You have to be right twice: when to sell and when to buy back
quiz.why: Getting out is only half the decision.

quiz.q: Many of the market's best days happen...
quiz.why: Big rebounds tend to cluster in volatile periods.

quiz.q: Which habit helps most investors?
a: Investing regularly and staying the course
quiz.why: Consistency lets compounding work.

lessons.title: The math of losses
cards: Losses and gains aren't symmetric. If you lose 50%, you need a 100% gain just to get back to where you started.

cards.text: Try it: slide the loss and see the gain you'd need to recover.

cards.q: Your $1,000 drops 20% one year and rises 20% the next. Where are you?
cards.why: $1,000 falls to $800, and 20% of $800 is only $160.

cards: That's why limiting big losses matters: diversify, avoid putting too much in one stock, and be careful with borrowed money (margin), which magnifies losses.

quiz.q: After a 50% loss, what gain gets you back to even?
quiz.why: Half your money has to double to recover.

quiz.q: Down 20%, then up 20%, leaves you...
quiz.why: The gain is on a smaller amount.

quiz.q: Which helps limit big losses?
quiz.why: Spreading out keeps one disaster from sinking you.

lessons.title: Your brain on money
cards: Investing is as much about behavior as numbers. Fear and greed push people to buy high and sell low, the opposite of what they want.

cards.text: Match each bias to what it looks like:
pairs: Losses hurt about twice as much as gains feel good
Only reading news that agrees with you

cards.q: A stock you own is down 30% and you feel sick about it. What's a good first step?
a: Re-check whether the business story has changed
Sell immediately to stop the pain
cards.why: Decide based on the business, not the feeling. A falling price alone doesn't tell you what to do.

cards: Simple guardrails help: write down why you bought a stock, decide in advance what would make you sell, and avoid checking prices constantly.

quiz.q: What is FOMO?
quiz.why: It pushes people to buy after big run-ups.

quiz.q: Loss aversion means...
a: Losses feel worse than equal gains feel good
quiz.why: Researchers found losses sting about twice as much.

quiz.q: Which guardrail helps against emotional decisions?
quiz.why: A written reason is something to check against later.

lessons.title: Asset allocation: your mix
cards: Asset allocation is how you split money between types of investments, like stocks, bonds and cash. It drives most of a portfolio's ups and downs.
Stocks have grown the most over long periods but swing hard. Bonds usually grow more slowly and steadily. Cash is the steadiest but loses ground to inflation.

cards.text: Order these from usually least to most volatile:
cards.why: Each step trades more stability for more potential growth.

cards.q: Someone needs their money in 2 years for a house down payment. Which mix fits better?
cards.why: Two years isn't enough time to reliably recover from a stock market drop.

cards: A common rule of thumb: the further away your goal, the more stock you can hold, because you have time to recover from drops. As the goal gets closer, many people shift toward bonds and cash.

quiz.q: What is asset allocation?
a: How you split money across types of investments
quiz.why: Your mix of stocks, bonds and cash.

quiz.q: Which usually swings the most?
quiz.why: Stocks carry the most risk and the most growth.

quiz.q: As a goal gets closer, many investors...
quiz.why: Less time to recover means less room for big swings.

lessons.title: Rebalancing
cards: Over time, winners grow and your mix drifts. A 60% stocks and 40% bonds portfolio can turn into 75/25 after a strong run, which is riskier than you planned.

cards.q: You aim for 60% stocks and 40% bonds. After a great year you have 70% stocks. What does rebalancing do?
a: Sell some stocks and buy bonds to get back to 60/40
cards.why: It moves you back to the risk level you chose.

cards: Rebalancing makes you trim what has risen and add to what has lagged: a built-in way to buy low and sell high.
Two common approaches: rebalance on a schedule, like once a year, or whenever your mix drifts more than about 5 percentage points. Adding new money to whatever is underweight avoids selling at all.
In taxable accounts, selling can trigger taxes, so many people rebalance with new contributions or inside retirement accounts.

quiz.q: Why rebalance?
a: To keep your risk where you planned it
quiz.why: Drift quietly changes how much risk you're taking.

quiz.q: Rebalancing usually means...
a: Trimming winners and adding to laggards
Buying more of whatever went up
quiz.why: It nudges you back to your target mix.

quiz.q: A way to rebalance without selling:
a: Put new money into what's underweight
quiz.why: New contributions can fix the mix with no sale and no tax.

lessons.title: Spotting scams and red flags
cards: If someone promises guaranteed high returns with no risk, it's a scam. Real investments always carry risk.

cards.text: Match each scam to how it works:
pairs: Hyping a cheap stock, then selling to the buyers
Paying old investors with new investors' money
Fake messages trying to steal your login
Crypto creators vanishing with investors' money

cards.q: A stranger messages you about a coin that "can't lose" and will "10x by Friday". What should you do?
a: Ignore it, it's a classic scam
Invest a little to test it
cards.why: Unsolicited messages, guarantees and deadlines are three red flags at once.

cards: Red flags: pressure to act fast, guaranteed returns, secret strategies, requests to pay in crypto or gift cards, and anyone asking for your password or wallet recovery phrase.
Check before you trust. In the US you can look up brokers and advisors on FINRA BrokerCheck, and report fraud to the SEC or the FTC.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag?
a: A company filing reports with the SEC
quiz.why: No real investment can guarantee high returns.

quiz.q: What is a pump and dump?
a: Hyping a stock in order to sell it to new buyers
quiz.why: The promoters profit, and the late buyers are left holding the drop.

quiz.q: Someone asks for your crypto wallet recovery phrase. You should...
a: Share it if they seem friendly
Post it to verify your account
quiz.why: Anyone with the phrase controls the wallet.

lessons.title: Bonds: lending for interest
cards: A bond is a loan. You lend money to a government or company, and they pay you interest and return the money on a set date, called maturity.
US Treasury bonds are considered among the safest because they're backed by the US government. Corporate bonds pay more interest because companies are riskier borrowers.

cards.q: Interest rates rise. What usually happens to the price of bonds you already own?
cards.why: New bonds now pay more, so older bonds paying less are worth less if you sell before maturity.

cards.text: A bond fund (AGG) versus two stock funds, in real numbers. Guess which swings the least.

cards: Many investors hold bonds to steady a portfolio. Bond funds and ETFs let you own hundreds of bonds in one purchase.

quiz.q: What is a bond?
a: A loan that pays you interest
quiz.why: You're the lender.

quiz.q: When rates rise, existing bond prices usually...
quiz.why: Older, lower-paying bonds become less attractive.

quiz.q: Why do corporate bonds pay more than Treasuries?
quiz.why: More risk means lenders demand more interest.

lessons.title: Crypto basics
cards: Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin are digital assets recorded on a public ledger called a blockchain. No company or government controls Bitcoin, and its supply is capped at 21 million coins.
Crypto prices are driven mostly by demand and sentiment. Coins don't earn profits like companies do, which makes them very hard to value.

cards.text: Guess which swings the least, then see the real yearly volatility.

cards.q: Bitcoin has fallen more than 70% from a high several times. If a drop like that would be too much for you, what makes sense?
a: Keep crypto a small slice, or skip it
cards.why: Only invest what you could watch fall a long way without being forced to sell.

cards: Keep it safe: use reputable exchanges, turn on two-factor authentication, and never share your recovery phrase.

quiz.q: What is a blockchain?
a: A public ledger that records transactions
quiz.why: Everyone can see the record, and no single party controls it.

quiz.q: Why is crypto hard to value?
quiz.why: There are no earnings to measure the price against.

quiz.q: Compared with the S&P 500, Bitcoin's price usually swings...
quiz.why: Its yearly volatility is typically several times the market's.

lessons.title: Options in plain English
cards: An option is a contract that gives you the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell a stock at a set price (the strike) before a set date (expiration).

cards.text: Match each term to what it means:
pairs: The right to buy at the strike price
The right to sell at the strike price
The price set in the contract
What you pay to buy the option

cards.q: You buy a call option with a $100 strike for $3 a share. The stock is at $95 when the option expires. What happens?
a: It expires worthless and you lose the $3
You must buy the stock at $100
cards.why: Nobody would use the right to buy at $100 when the stock costs $95, so the option is worth nothing.

cards: Options can magnify gains and losses, and many expire worthless. Most beginners are better off understanding stocks well first.

quiz.q: A call option gives you the right to...
quiz.why: Calls are for buying, puts are for selling.

quiz.q: If an option expires worthless, the buyer loses...
quiz.why: The premium is the most an option buyer can lose.

quiz.q: What is the strike price?
a: The price set in the option contract
quiz.why: It's the price you have the right to buy or sell at.

lessons.title: Short selling
cards: Short selling is betting a stock will fall. You borrow shares, sell them now, and hope to buy them back cheaper later to return them.

cards.q: You short a stock at $50 and it rises to $80. What's your loss per share?
cards.why: You sold at $50 and must buy back at $80.

cards: The risk is lopsided. A stock can only fall to $0, so a short's gain is capped, but a stock can keep rising, so the possible loss has no limit.
A short squeeze happens when a heavily shorted stock rises and short sellers rush to buy back, pushing it even higher. GameStop in early 2021 is a famous example.

quiz.q: Short sellers profit when a stock...
quiz.why: They sell first and buy back cheaper.

quiz.q: Why is shorting risky?
quiz.why: There's no ceiling on how high a price can go.

quiz.q: What is a short squeeze?
a: Short sellers buying back fast, pushing the price up
quiz.why: Their buying adds fuel to the rise.

lessons.title: IPOs: when companies go public
cards: An initial public offering (IPO) is when a private company first sells shares to the public and starts trading on an exchange.
Companies go public to raise money and to let early investors and employees sell. Banks help set the starting price.

cards.q: A hyped IPO jumps 60% on its first day. What tends to happen afterwards?
a: It varies a lot, and many lag the market in later years
It always falls back to the IPO price
cards.why: Studies of IPOs find that, on average, they trail the broader market over the following few years.

cards: New public companies have short track records and often sell more shares later. Insiders are usually locked up for about six months after the IPO, and prices can drop when that lockup ends.

quiz.q: What is an IPO?
a: A company's first sale of shares to the public
quiz.why: It's the moment a private company becomes public.

quiz.q: Why do companies go public?
a: To raise money and let early owners sell
quiz.why: Public companies must report results every quarter, too.

quiz.q: What is a lockup period?
a: A time when insiders can't sell
quiz.why: It usually lasts about six months after the IPO.

lessons.title: REITs: real estate on the stock market
cards: A REIT (real estate investment trust) owns income-producing property, like apartments, warehouses, cell towers or data centers, and trades like a stock.
To qualify, US REITs must pay out at least 90% of their taxable income as dividends, which is why many have high yields.

cards.text: Two REITs and the S&P 500. Guess which pays the highest yield.

cards.q: Interest rates rise sharply. What often happens to REIT prices?
cards.why: REITs borrow a lot and compete with bonds for income investors, so rising rates tend to weigh on them.

cards: REITs let you own a slice of real estate without being a landlord, but they still swing with the stock market.

quiz.q: What does a REIT own?
quiz.why: Property that earns rent.

quiz.q: Why do REITs often have high yields?
a: They must pay out most of their taxable income
quiz.why: The 90% payout rule.

quiz.q: Rising interest rates often...
quiz.why: Borrowing costs more and bonds become competition.
